extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of literature/poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and evaluating tragic and epic poems: unity of action, choice of metre and diction, use of the wonderful, handling of improbable or irrational elements, and methods for resolving critical objections. Emphasises genre-appropriate language, plot structure, and artistic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a great matter to observe propriety in these several modes of expression, as also in compound words, strange (or rare) words, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe appropriateness across compound words, rare words, and other modes; the correct choice of these gives distinction to style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius, for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor is a high-level skill indicating genius; cultivate an eye for resemblances—cannot be simply taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to Dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In iambic verse...the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match word types to genre: compounds for dithyrambs, rare words for heroic/epic, metaphors for iambic; iambic seeks familiar speech and prose vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem/play should imitate a single whole action so it resembles a living organism; avoid treating a single period containing many loosely related events as a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale/length
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards scale or length, we have already laid down an adequate limit:—the beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the work small enough that beginning and end can be grasped within a single view; excessive length risks loss of unity and dilution of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: He detaches a single portion, and admits as episodes many events from the general story of the war—thus diversifying the poem...these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may admit episodes from a larger story to diversify and add dignity, but only if they are relevant and do not destroy unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: For of all measures the heroic is the stateliest and the most massive; and hence it most readily admits rare words and metaphors...Hence no one has ever composed a poem on a great scale in any other than heroic verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heroic metre for large-scale narrative; avoid mixing different metres (which is absurd and incongruous). Let the nature of the genre guide metre choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal poetial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator...Homer, after a few prefatory words, at once brings in a man, or woman, or other personage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive first-person authorial presence; let characters enact and reveal qualities rather than prolonged authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the wonderful and the probable impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy...Accordingly, the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include wonderful or seemingly impossible elements if they are probable within the art's demands and contribute to the effect; the mind accepts probable impossibilities more readily than improbable possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational parts from the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts. Everything irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or, at all events, it should lie outside the action of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build the plot from irrational incidents; if irrational elements exist they should be justified or placed outside the core dramatic action (e.g., a character's ignorance that is external to the action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. For, conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate diction for moments when action pauses; keep language clear during active expression of character and thought to avoid obscuring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential vs accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults, those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental...If a poet has chosen to imitate something, (but has imitated it incorrectly) through want of capacity, the error is inherent in the poetry. But if the failure is due to a wrong choice...the error is not essential to the poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing, determine whether faults affect the essence (e.g., wrong imitation) or are accidental (e.g., technical mistakes); essential faults are more serious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities by artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If he describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained...If, however, the end might have been as well, or better, attained without violating the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only permit impossible descriptions when they achieve the artistic aim and no better (rule-abiding) alternative exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider speaker, audience, timing, means and ends
rubrics_metrics.description: We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, by what means, or for what end...whether, for instance, it be to secure a greater good, or avert a greater evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions and speeches in context—who speaks, to whom, when, by what means, and to what purpose—before judging poetic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve critical difficulties by language features
rubrics_metrics.description: Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard to the usage of language. We may note a rare word...So, again, of Dolon...It is not meant that his body was ill-shaped, but that his face was ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent problems can often be explained by rare word meanings, metaphorical usage, accent or breathing, punctuation, ambiguity, or conventional usage; examine these before condemning a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accent, punctuation, ambiguity, and usage as interpretive tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Or again, the question may be solved by punctuation...Or again, by ambiguity of meaning...Or by the usage of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for interpretive fixes in accentuation, punctuation, multiple senses of a word, or idiomatic usage when lines seem problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret apparent contradictions by sense and relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply dialectical analysis: check whether terms are used with the same meaning, in the same relation and sense before declaring contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure irrationality and depravity absent inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce depraved or irrational character traits unless they are necessary to the inner logic of the plot or to attain the poem's ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize objections to poetry (five sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When answering critics, search for solutions under the twelve heads previously mentioned and classify objections into these five types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy vs Epic: unity, scale and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry differs from Tragedy in the scale on which it is constructed, and in its metre...Tragedy...attains its end within narrower limits; for the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one which is spread over a long time and so diluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize differences: epic can present simultaneous events and broader scale (heroic metre), while tragedy's concentrated unity and narrower limits often yield superior, focused effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid faults of performance being mistaken for faults of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: This censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; for gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation...Such was the fault found in Callippides...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between failings of actors/performers (overdone gesture, degraded representation) and failings of the poetic work itself when criticizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative form permits presentation of simultaneous events
rubrics_metrics.description: In Epic poetry, owing to the narrative form, many events simultaneously transacted can be presented; and these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative's freedom to present concurrent actions for grandeur and relief from sameness, but ensure relevance and preserve unity.
